script.opening: “Hello doctor. I’ve got another water infection, I know the feeling. And there was blood again yesterday. They told me at the hospital I’m fine — but I’m clearly not fine, am I?”

facts.text: “Two days. Burning when I pass water, going every half hour, and yesterday it was pink. Same as all the others.”
No fever, no shivers, no back or side pain, no sickness. You feel fine apart from the burning.

facts.topic: Pattern (only if asked whether anything sets them off)
facts.text: Pause. “I’ve… noticed they tend to come a day or two after… I have a partner now. Clive. We’ve been together a year.” Look embarrassed.
“It’s very dry down there since the breast cancer tablets. Sex is sore, to be honest.” No bleeding from the vagina, no unusual discharge, no lump or dragging feeling.

facts.topic: Washing (only if asked about hygiene or what you do after sex)
facts.text: “I wash inside with a feminine wash afterwards, to keep clean. A scented one.” You do not pass urine straight after sex.
“About three cups of tea a day. I don’t drink much water — I don’t want to be running to the loo when I’m out.”
Occasional small leak when you sneeze. No problems emptying.
One partner, Clive, for a year; before that only your late husband. No previous STIs. Happy to have a test if the doctor thinks it’s sensible.
“All clear at my last check in March. I take the letrozole every day. They said maybe five years, maybe longer.” No new lumps, bone pain, weight loss or cough.

facts.topic: Weight, appetite, bowels (answer no if asked)
facts.text: No weight loss, no night sweats, normal bowels.
Widowed three years ago. Retired school administrator, sings in a church choir. Never smoked. Alcohol: a glass of wine on Sundays.

Start frustrated and anxious about the blood and cancer. You only mention Clive and the dryness if asked about triggers or vaginal symptoms, and you find it embarrassing. If the doctor is matter-of-fact and kind, relax and talk openly. If oestrogen cream is mentioned, say: “I thought I wasn’t allowed hormones because of the breast cancer?” If told to stop having sex, become upset: “I’ve only just got a bit of life back.”

ice.ideas: “Something must be wrong inside — maybe they missed something.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the infections follow sex with her new partner, and sex has become painful since letrozole; she is embarrassed and worried she will have to give up the relationship. Underneath is fear that the blood means cancer — her breast cancer back, or bladder cancer the hospital missed.
ice.expectations: Antibiotics today and “a proper answer” — perhaps referral back to the hospital.

cues: “I’m clearly not fine, am I?” — frustration and fear after normal tests.
“I have a partner now.” — the post-coital pattern and her embarrassment.

checkpoints.text: Confirms an acute lower UTI and excludes upper-tract or systemic features (fever, rigors, loin pain, vomiting); checks previous culture sensitivities and response
Explores triggers sensitively and finds the post-coital pattern, vaginal dryness and dyspareunia on letrozole, douching with scented products, low fluid intake
Asks about red flags and other causes: postmenopausal bleeding, discharge, prolapse, incontinence or incomplete emptying, weight loss, breast cancer recurrence symptoms; considers STI testing

Treats the acute episode: midstream urine for culture before starting nitrofurantoin 100 mg modified-release twice daily for 3 days (renal function adequate); no dipstick reliance; repeat urinalysis after treatment to confirm the haematuria has resolved, with re-referral if it persists

Explains prevention: stop douching and scented products, pass urine after sex, hydration; non-hormonal vaginal moisturiser and lubricant now; vaginal oestrogen discussed with her breast team because she takes an aromatase inhibitor

Offers single-dose post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis (nitrofurantoin 100 mg within 2 hours of sex) with risks (resistance, side effects), mentions methenamine hippurate as a later non-antibiotic option, and offers a face-to-face pelvic examination; safety-nets for pyelonephritis or sepsis
Acknowledges her frustration and fear about cancer and explains what the normal CT and cystoscopy do and do not mean, without dismissing her
Discusses sex and the new relationship in a matter-of-fact, non-judgemental way, supports her wish to continue it, and shares decisions about prophylaxis

worked.txt: “It must be exhausting to keep getting these after being told everything looks normal. Let’s sort out today’s infection, then work out why they keep coming back.”
“Some women notice the infections come after sex — is that something you’ve noticed? I ask everyone, because there’s a lot we can do about it.”

“Blood in the urine with an infection is very common — the infection inflames the bladder lining. Your camera test three weeks ago looked directly at the bladder and was normal, and the scan showed healthy kidneys. That makes cancer very unlikely. To be thorough, I’ll recheck your urine once the infection has cleared — if blood is still there, I’ll speak to the urologists.”

“Vaginal oestrogen helps prevent infections, but because you take letrozole it may reduce how well the letrozole works, so it’s a decision to make with your breast team. In the meantime, a non-hormonal moisturiser and a lubricant can make a real difference.”

“Another option is a single nitrofurantoin tablet within two hours after sex. It works well, but any regular antibiotic carries a risk of resistance and side effects, so we’d review it after six months.”
“If you get a temperature, shivers, pain in your back or side, or you’re being sick, call us the same day or 111 — that could mean it’s gone to the kidney.”

f.learning: Recurrent UTI (two or more in six months, or three or more in twelve) needs a search for modifiable causes once structural disease has been excluded — and the commonest are found in the history, not the scan: post-coital timing, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, douching or spermicides, low fluid intake, incontinence and incomplete emptying. In women with recurrent UTI, send urine for culture rather than relying on dipstick. Visible haematuria during a proven infection, with a normal cystoscopy and CT urogram three weeks earlier, is very likely inflammatory, but repeat urinalysis after treatment closes the loop. NICE NG112 (updated 2024) sets out the prevention ladder: behavioural and personal-hygiene advice; vaginal oestrogen for postmenopausal women; single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis after exposure to a trigger, or daily prophylaxis; and methenamine hippurate as an alternative to daily antibiotics. Here the complication is an aromatase inhibitor: NICE NG23 advises non-hormonal treatments first and, for women on aromatase inhibitors, agreeing options for persistent genitourinary symptoms with the breast cancer specialist. Talking about sex plainly and positively — especially with an older woman in a new relationship — is part of good clinical care.

knowledge.summary: Treat today’s UTI after sending a culture; recheck the urine for blood once treated; then prevention — behaviour, non-hormonal vaginal products, oestrogen only via the breast team, post-coital prophylaxis, methenamine later.

points.t: Recurrent UTI: two or more episodes in 6 months or three or more in 12 months. Culture each episode; refer men, and women with recurrent upper UTI, uncertain diagnosis or red flags such as persistent visible haematuria after treatment. Do not use dipstick to diagnose UTI in women with recurrent infection — send a midstream urine.

Nitrofurantoin modified-release 100 mg twice daily for 3 days if eGFR is 45 or above (NICE NG109; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: nitrofurantoin). Choose by previous sensitivities — trimethoprim resistance documented here.

Avoid douching and scented products; do not delay voiding; pass urine after sex; adequate hydration; wipe front to back. Evidence for cranberry products and D-mannose is limited and uncertain — NICE allows self-care discussion, not prescribing.

points.h: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause and aromatase inhibitors
points.t: Non-hormonal vaginal moisturisers and lubricants first. Vaginal oestrogen reduces recurrent UTI in postmenopausal women, but for women taking aromatase inhibitors NICE NG23 advises working with the breast cancer specialist on options for persistent symptoms, as vaginal oestrogen may reduce aromatase-inhibitor efficacy.

Single dose within 2 hours of a trigger such as sex: nitrofurantoin 100 mg (if eGFR 45 or above) or trimethoprim 200 mg if sensitive. Usual adult dose as stated (NICE NG112; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: nitrofurantoin). Discuss resistance, side effects, and long-term nitrofurantoin risks (pulmonary and hepatic reactions, peripheral neuropathy); review at 6 months.

An alternative to daily antibiotic prophylaxis when behavioural measures, vaginal oestrogen or single-dose prophylaxis have not been effective or are unsuitable. Usual adult dose: 1 g twice daily (NICE NG112; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: methenamine hippurate). Avoid urine alkalinisers; review within 6 months.
Offer a pelvic examination (atrophy, prolapse, masses) and consider STI testing if risk; check post-void residual if voiding symptoms (done here: 30 mL).
The Clear pass candidate asks about sex comfortably, explains the haematuria honestly with a plan to recheck, and knows that the oestrogen decision sits with the breast team without dismissing it.

model.text: Hello Mrs Baptiste, it’s Dr Rowe. Can you see and hear me? Are you somewhere private to talk?
model.why: Video set-up and privacy before an intimate history

model.text: Yes. It’s another water infection — and blood again. The hospital said I’m fine, but I’m clearly not.
That sounds really frustrating. Let’s sort today out, and then try to understand why they keep coming back. Tell me about the last couple of days.
Burning, going every half hour, and it was pink yesterday.
Any temperature, shivers, pain in your back or sides, or sickness?
Have you noticed anything that sets them off? Some women find they come after sex — I ask everyone.
Well… yes. I’ve a new partner. They come a day or two after. And it’s very dry since the breast tablets — it’s sore.
Thank you for telling me — that’s really useful. What do you do afterwards — wash, pass water? Any bleeding from the vagina, discharge, or a dragging feeling?
model.why: Hygiene practices; postmenopausal bleeding and prolapse screen

model.text: I wash inside with a scented wash. No bleeding or discharge.
And how have you been otherwise — weight, appetite, any lumps or bone pain? I know the blood worries you.
All fine. But I keep thinking it’s cancer — that the hospital missed it, or the breast cancer’s back.

That’s a very understandable fear. Infection inflames the bladder lining and often causes blood. Three weeks ago the camera looked directly inside your bladder and it was normal, and the scan of your kidneys was normal too — so cancer is very unlikely. I’ll recheck your urine after this infection; if blood is still there, I’ll go back to the urologists.
model.why: Honest reassurance plus a plan that closes the loop

model.text: For today: a urine sample to the lab first, then nitrofurantoin twice a day for three days — it’s worked for you before.
model.why: Culture then treat according to sensitivities

model.text: I think the dryness and the timing after sex are the key. Stop the internal washing — it removes the protective bacteria. Pass water soon after sex and drink a bit more water. A vaginal moisturiser and a lubricant should make sex more comfortable.
What about oestrogen cream? I thought I couldn’t have hormones.

It does help prevent infections, but with letrozole it may make the letrozole work less well, so I’ll write to your breast team so you can decide together. Another option is one nitrofurantoin tablet within two hours after sex — effective, but antibiotics carry a risk of resistance, so we’d review it in six months. And there’s a non-antibiotic tablet, methenamine, if these don’t work.

I’d also like to examine you in person next week to check for dryness or a prolapse. If you get a temperature, shivers, back pain or vomiting, call us the same day or 111. What will you do from today?
Urine sample, start the tablets, no more scented wash, get a moisturiser, and you’ll write to the breast team. And I don’t have to give up Clive.

social.t: New relationships after bereavement are common; older women are often not asked about sex and may not volunteer it. Asking normalises it and unlocks the diagnosis.
Douching and scented washes are often done “to be clean” and to reduce infections, but they disrupt protective vaginal flora.

legal.t: Writing to the breast team is direct care; explain it and record her agreement.

professional.t: Discharge from urology is not the end of the problem — the GP owns the prevention plan and coordinates with oncology about hormones.
Prophylaxis is a shared decision with a review date; record the indication and stop date.

community.t: Breast cancer nurse specialists can advise on vaginal dryness during endocrine therapy; Breast Cancer Now has information on sex and intimacy after treatment.

psychosocial: Choir and social life — fluid restriction when out
core: Normal CT urogram and cystoscopy 3 weeks ago

playbook.diagnosis: Acute lower UTI on a background of recurrent post-coital UTI, contributed to by genitourinary syndrome of menopause (aromatase-inhibitor related), douching and low fluid intake; structural causes excluded.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This is another bladder infection. The tests show your bladder and kidneys are healthy. The infections seem to be set off by sex, made more likely by dryness from your breast tablets — and that’s something we can work on.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something had been missed and that the blood meant cancer — the tests make that very unlikely and I’ll recheck the urine. And you don’t need to give up your relationship to get on top of this.”
management.psychosocial: Practical fluid advice for choir days; sensitive discussion of sex and lubrication; breast-nurse support.
sharedPlan: MSU then nitrofurantoin MR 100 mg twice daily for 3 days
Repeat urinalysis 1–2 weeks after treatment; re-refer if haematuria persists
Stop douching and scented products; void after sex; more water
Non-hormonal moisturiser and lubricant; letter to breast team about vaginal oestrogen
Post-coital nitrofurantoin 100 mg single dose — review at 6 months; methenamine later if needed
safetyNet: Fever, rigors, loin pain, vomiting — same day or NHS 111
Symptoms not improving in 48 hours — call back
Visible blood without infection symptoms — tell us

pitfalls.intro: Candidates either treat the infection and stop, or re-refer to urology because of the blood without finding the obvious modifiable causes.

items.fail: Never asks about sex, vaginal symptoms or washing habits.
items.why: The post-coital pattern and genitourinary syndrome of menopause are the main treatable drivers here.
items.fix: Ask every woman with recurrent UTI about triggers, in a normalising way.

items.fail: Prescribes vaginal oestrogen straight away without considering the aromatase inhibitor — or flatly refuses it as “banned after breast cancer”.
items.why: Both are wrong: it is an option, but on an aromatase inhibitor the decision belongs with the breast team (NICE NG23).
items.fix: Start non-hormonal products and write to oncology.

items.fail: Tells her the hospital tests were normal so there is “nothing to worry about” and moves on.
items.why: It dismisses her fear and her lived experience; she leaves without a plan for the blood.
items.fix: Explain what the tests show, recheck the urine after treatment, and say what would trigger re-referral.

timeMap.d: Acute symptoms and upper-tract screen; triggers; vaginal symptoms; washing; red flags.
Haematuria and the normal tests; MSU then nitrofurantoin.
Behaviour, moisturiser and lubricant, breast team re oestrogen, post-coital prophylaxis, methenamine later.

wordPics.clearFail: Gives another antibiotic course by dipstick logic and re-refers to urology; never asks about sex or vaginal symptoms; prescribes oestrogen without thought to letrozole; no safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Treats appropriately and gives generic hygiene advice, but misses the post-coital pattern or the aromatase-inhibitor issue, and leaves the cancer worry unaddressed.
wordPics.pass: Culture and nitrofurantoin; finds the post-coital pattern and dryness; non-hormonal measures; oncology input for vaginal oestrogen; offers post-coital prophylaxis; addresses haematuria with a recheck plan; safety-nets.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass with sensitivity and pace: normalises talk about sex, stops the douching, explains the tests and residual uncertainty honestly, shares the prophylaxis decision with numbers on risks, offers examination, and closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “The tests were normal, so there’s nothing serious going on.”
avoid.instead: “The tests make cancer very unlikely; I’ll recheck your urine once this has cleared to be sure.”
“Let’s make sex more comfortable and less likely to trigger infections.”
avoid.why: Respects her relationship; targets the cause.

avoid.dont: “You can’t have hormones after breast cancer.”
avoid.instead: “Vaginal oestrogen is possible for some women, but with letrozole we need your breast team’s view.”
avoid.why: Accurate and keeps the option open.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
